title: Database Index Fundamentals
description: Understand what database indexes do, how they speed up reads, and what they cost.
learningObjectives: Explain what a database index is and why a database may use one.
Describe the basic idea behind a B-tree index.
Recognize query patterns that can benefit from an index.
Explain the read-performance, storage, and write-performance trade-offs of indexes.
Use a PostgreSQL EXPLAIN plan at a basic level to investigate query access.
Explain where PostgreSQL stores index data, how caching works, and what indexes cost in disk and memory.

mentalModel.text: Imagine a contacts table with a million people. Without an index, finding one email may mean checking many rows. An index is like an ordered lookup list that helps the database jump toward matching rows. It can make reads faster, but the database must keep that list updated whenever the table changes.

blocks.text: An index is a separate lookup structure, like the index at the back of a book: it maps a searchable key to the location of matching table rows, so the database may avoid checking every table row. In PostgreSQL, the index has its own persistent pages on disk; frequently used pages may also be cached in shared_buffers or the operating system's page cache. An index makes a query eligible for a faster path, but does not force the planner to use it.

blocks.title: Create an index in PostgreSQL

blocks.text:
Key idea

The index can help locate rows matching the email predicate. It does not guarantee that the planner will choose the index for every query.

blocks.problem: An API repeatedly finds a user by email in a table with one million users.
reasoning: Without an index, PostgreSQL may need to inspect many rows to find the email.
A B-tree index on email can navigate to the matching key, then locate the table row if the query needs other columns.
The index is separate from the table and must be maintained when indexed values change.
blocks.outcome: An index is a shortcut to matching rows, not a second copy of the whole table and not a guarantee that every query will use it.

concepts.title: Why indexes can speed up reads

blocks.text: An index helps most when it avoids enough table work to repay the cost of looking up keys and fetching matching rows.

Without an index, the database may check every row to find a few matches. With a suitable index, it can go straight to the relevant keys. The speed-up depends on how many rows match, how large the table is, and how much extra work is needed to fetch those rows.

blocks.title: Filter on an indexed column
When the index may not help
blocks.content: If a query returns a very large fraction of a small table, scanning the table may be cheaper than using the index and then fetching many rows.

blocks.problem: An endpoint fetches one order out of two million using order_id.
reasoning: A unique index can find the matching key with only a small number of page visits.
The database then fetches the requested row if its columns are not already available in the index.
For a query that returns most orders, many row fetches may cost more than scanning table pages in sequence.
blocks.outcome: Index benefit depends on the fraction of rows returned and the work needed after the lookup.

blocks.text: A B-tree is PostgreSQL's usual default index. It keeps keys sorted across balanced pages; separator keys direct the search to child pages until the leaf that can contain the key is reached. Its order also supports range conditions and compatible sorting.

blocks.title: Equality and range filters
How a B-tree narrows a search
rows: Compare the target key with separator keys.
Repeat comparisons at the next level.
Find the key or the insertion/search position.
Reach matching entries without scanning every key.

blocks.title: Simplified B-tree search for key 25
blocks.alt: A root node with keys 20 and 40 routes the search for 25 to the middle child, which contains keys 22, 25, and 30.

steps.title: Compare at the root
steps.description: 25 is greater than 20 and less than 40, so follow the middle child.

steps.title: Inspect the selected leaf
steps.description: The leaf contains 22, 25, and 30. The target key 25 is found.

blocks.problem: A products table has an index on price and a query asks for prices between 100 and 500 in ascending order.
reasoning: PostgreSQL navigates to the first key in the requested range.
It walks the matching leaf entries in key order until the range ends.
Because the index order matches ORDER BY price, PostgreSQL may avoid a separate sort.
blocks.outcome: B-trees support equality lookups, range scans, and compatible ordering. They are the usual starting point for scalar columns.

blocks.prompt: Does a B-tree lookup need to inspect every key in every leaf?
blocks.explanation: The balanced hierarchy narrows the search to a relevant path, although the exact physical work depends on the database, tree shape, and cache state.

blocks.text: Build indexes around the queries the application actually runs, including their filters, joins, sort order, and limits.

An index should fit queries the application actually runs. If a common query filters by customer_id and sorts by created_at, an index on (customer_id, created_at) may help. The order matters: an index starting with a different column may not provide the same shortcut.

blocks.title: Composite index
blocks.source:
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer_created
ON orders (customer_id, created_at DESC);

SELECT id, created_at
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 42
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 10;

blocks.problem: A customer page runs `WHERE customer_id = 42 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20`.
reasoning: An index on (customer_id, created_at DESC) narrows to that customer and provides newest-first order.
The database may stop after finding 20 qualifying rows instead of sorting every order for that customer.
An index beginning with a different column may not provide the same efficient path.
blocks.outcome: Choose column order from the whole query shape, not from a list of columns that seem important.

blocks.text: Every index speeds only some operations and creates work for writes, storage, memory, and maintenance.

Indexes take space and need maintenance. Each insert, delete, or update may also change one or more indexes. Too many indexes can make writes slower and use memory that could otherwise hold useful data.

blocks.title: Write-heavy table
blocks.content: If a table receives frequent inserts and updates, measure the value of each index. Keep indexes that support important query patterns and revisit redundant or unused indexes carefully.

blocks.problem: A write-heavy events table has six indexes, but only two support frequent queries.
reasoning: Each insert must add entries to relevant indexes; updates can also change index entries.
The extra indexes consume disk and cache space and add WAL and maintenance work.
Check actual index usage and workload before dropping an index, because rare administrative queries may still depend on it.
blocks.outcome: Keep indexes that pay for themselves in the real workload; more indexes are not automatically better.

blocks.text: Selectivity is the fraction of rows matching a predicate. Searching for one rare email is highly selective; searching for a status shared by half the table is not. PostgreSQL estimates matching rows and compares the cost of index navigation plus heap fetches with alternatives such as a sequential or bitmap scan.

blocks.title: Inspect a query plan
blocks.source:
EXPLAIN
SELECT *
FROM users
WHERE email = 'sam@example.com';

blocks.text:
Plan interpretation

Look for nodes such as Seq Scan, Index Scan, Index Only Scan, or Bitmap Index Scan. EXPLAIN shows the planned operations; EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the query and reports actual timings and row counts, so use it thoughtfully.

blocks.problem: An email lookup returns one row, but a status filter returns 800,000 of one million rows.
reasoning: The email lookup is highly selective, so an index is likely to avoid most table work.
The status filter matches most of the table, so a sequential scan may be cheaper.
Use EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) to compare estimates with actual rows and inspect the work performed.
blocks.outcome: The planner chooses based on estimated cost. An index can be useful for one predicate and unhelpful for another.

blocks.text: The key idea is simple: an index scan uses an index to find matching rows; a sequential scan reads through the table's pages and checks which rows match. Neither is always better. PostgreSQL chooses based on how much data it expects to read and how expensive each approach will be.

## 1. Index scan

Suppose a users table has one million rows and an index on email:

blocks.title: What happens during an index scan

steps.title: Search the index
steps.description: PostgreSQL navigates the index to find the email key instead of checking every user row.

steps.title: Locate the table row
steps.description: The index entry identifies where the matching row can be found in the table.

steps.title: Fetch the requested data
steps.description: If the index does not contain every column the query needs, PostgreSQL visits the table to read the rest of the row.

blocks.text: The advantage is that PostgreSQL may avoid reading most of the table. For a B-tree index, finding a key takes roughly logarithmic navigation through the index, followed by any necessary row fetches. Actual performance also depends on page reads, caching, and how many rows match.

## 2. Sequential scan

Now consider a query that returns most of the users:

blocks.title: Find active users

blocks.text: Imagine 900,000 of the one million users are active. An index on is_active could identify those rows, but PostgreSQL might then need to fetch a very large number of table rows. Reading the table's pages in sequence can be cheaper than jumping between many separate row locations.
A sequential scan does not mean reading each row individually from disk. PostgreSQL reads table pages and checks the rows in those pages. Some pages may already be cached in memory.

blocks.title: When each approach tends to make sense
rows: Find one user by unique email
Only a small subset of the table is needed.
Reading pages in sequence can cost less than fetching most rows through an index.
Read every row for a report
The query needs nearly all the data anyway.

blocks.text: These are common patterns, not guarantees. The planner also considers table size, statistics, available indexes, cache state, and the query itself.

## 3. Check the actual plan

In PostgreSQL, inspect a representative query with EXPLAIN ANALYZE:

blocks.title: Inspect an email lookup
blocks.source:
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT *
FROM users
WHERE email = 'aman@example.com';

blocks.text:
Look for these plan nodes:

- `Index Scan` — uses an index and may fetch rows from the table.
- `Seq Scan` — reads table pages sequentially and checks rows.
- `Index Only Scan` — can return data from the index without fetching the table for every row, when the index contains the requested values and PostgreSQL's visibility information permits it.

`EXPLAIN ANALYZE` actually executes the query. Be careful with expensive queries and statements that modify data; use a safe test environment or transaction when appropriate.
Use the plan and a representative workload to test whether an index solves the real bottleneck.

Start with a real query that is slow or important. Check its plan, identify what it filters and sorts, then test an index that fits. Compare read speed and write cost; never add an index just because a column looks important.

A practical workflow

1. Capture the query and its parameters.
2. Inspect EXPLAIN or EXPLAIN ANALYZE where safe.
3. Check row estimates, actual rows, and scan type.
4. Propose an index that matches the query pattern.
5. Compare representative performance and write overhead.

blocks.problem: A query is slow and someone suggests adding an index to every column in its WHERE clause.
reasoning: Capture the exact query and representative parameter values.
Inspect the plan to see whether the cost comes from scanning too many rows, repeated joins, sorting, or fetching heap rows.
Test one index candidate, compare read latency and buffer activity, and measure the write overhead.
blocks.outcome: A useful index is one that improves the workload enough to justify its ongoing cost.

blocks.title: Read EXPLAIN ANALYZE carefully
blocks.content: EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the statement. For a slow SELECT, it performs the read; for an INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE, it can change data. Test write statements in a safe transaction or test environment, and remember that timing from a small or warm-cache test may not represent production.

concepts.title: Where indexes live: disk space and memory

blocks.text: An index is a persistent database structure, not just a setting and not something that exists only in RAM. In PostgreSQL, table rows and index entries are stored in database files on persistent storage. The index has its own pages and consumes disk space in addition to the table.

When PostgreSQL reads a table or index page, it can keep that page in shared_buffers. The operating system may also cache file pages in memory. A later lookup may reuse a cached page instead of waiting for storage. So an index consumes disk space whether or not it is cached, and its frequently used pages may also consume memory.

blocks.problem: A users table is 2 GB, and its email index is 400 MB. The application repeatedly looks up users by email.
reasoning: The table and index both occupy persistent storage; the index adds 400 MB rather than replacing the table.
Frequently used index pages may stay in memory, making later lookups faster than cold reads.
If the index is much larger than available cache, lookups may require more storage reads. Other workloads also compete for memory.
blocks.outcome: Think of an index as an extra on-disk data structure whose hot pages may be cached. More indexes improve some reads but increase storage, memory pressure, and write work.

blocks.text: 1. Problem and motivation — A service looks up one user by email in a million-row table. Reading every row is unnecessary, but the lookup structure takes disk space and must be maintained when data changes.

2. Definition and design choice — An index is a persistent lookup structure stored separately from table rows. Its pages use disk space and may also be cached in PostgreSQL shared buffers or the operating system page cache. An index does not mean all data is in RAM.

steps.title: What is a database index?
steps.description: An index is an extra lookup structure that helps PostgreSQL find rows without checking every row in the table.

steps.title: Why indexes can speed up reads
steps.description: An index helps most when it avoids enough table work to repay the cost of looking up keys and fetching matching rows.

steps.title: B-tree indexes
steps.description: A B-tree keeps keys sorted across balanced pages. The database narrows the possible key range at each level until it reaches the relevant leaf.

steps.title: Match indexes to query patterns
steps.description: Build indexes around the queries the application actually runs, including their filters, joins, sort order, and limits.

blocks.problem: A unique email lookup returns one row from a million, while a report returns 700,000 rows.
reasoning: The B-tree lookup visits a few index pages and may fetch a heap page; a broad report may be cheaper with a sequential scan because many scattered rows cost more to fetch.
Cached page work can be on microsecond scales, while a cold random SSD read is often tens to hundreds of microseconds. These are rough hardware-dependent scales, not latency guarantees.
Every index occupies persistent storage and adds work to inserts and relevant updates. Indexes can also compete for memory cache.
blocks.outcome: Explain the lookup path and disk/cache distinction, then validate with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) and measure read latency plus write overhead.

blocks.title: 5. Anti-pattern to avoid
blocks.content: An index makes some access patterns cheaper; it does not make every query faster.

blocks.prompt: 6. Interview probe — What is the primary purpose of a database index?
blocks.answer: An index provides an additional access structure that can help the database find matching rows without examining the entire table. It does not replace the table or guarantee a particular runtime. Uniqueness is enforced only by a suitable unique constraint or unique index.
blocks.explanation: A strong interview answer states the problem, walks through the mechanism, names assumptions and trade-offs, and describes how to verify the result rather than relying on a rule of thumb.

tradeoffsAndPitfalls.text: An index makes some access patterns cheaper; it does not make every query faster.
PostgreSQL's planner may choose a sequential scan when it estimates that scanning the table is cheaper.
A composite B-tree index's column order matters; an index on (a, b) is not equivalent to an index on (b, a).
Indexes increase storage use and can add overhead to inserts, deletes, and updates.
Low-selectivity predicates may not benefit from an ordinary index, depending on the table and query.
EXPLAIN shows the planned operations; EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the query, so be careful with expensive or side-effecting statements.
Do not assume all databases use the same index types, storage structures, or query-planner rules.

revisionSheet.text: An index is an auxiliary data structure that helps locate rows efficiently.
PostgreSQL uses B-tree by default; it supports equality, range and ordered access patterns.
Index usefulness depends on the query, selectivity, data distribution, table size and cost estimates.
The query planner chooses a plan; the mere existence of an index does not guarantee index usage.
Indexes trade storage and write overhead for potential read improvements.
Use EXPLAIN to inspect a plan and EXPLAIN ANALYZE to measure actual execution.
Design indexes from real workload patterns and validate with measurements.

questions.prompt: What is the primary purpose of a database index?

options.text: To eliminate the need for storing table rows
To help the database locate matching rows more efficiently
To guarantee that every query runs in constant time
To automatically prevent duplicate values in every column

questions.explanation: An index provides an additional access structure that can help the database find matching rows without examining the entire table. It does not replace the table or guarantee a particular runtime. Uniqueness is enforced only by a suitable unique constraint or unique index.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, which index type is the default and commonly supports equality and range comparisons?

options.text: B-tree
GIN only
BRIN only
Hash is the default for every index

questions.explanation: B-tree is PostgreSQL's default index type and supports common equality, range, and ordered-access patterns. GIN and BRIN are useful for different data and workload patterns.

questions.prompt: If a PostgreSQL table has an index on a column, PostgreSQL must use that index whenever a query filters on the column.
questions.explanation: The planner estimates the costs of available plans. If a sequential scan is expected to be cheaper—for example, when many rows must be read—it may choose that instead.

questions.prompt: Which are common costs or trade-offs of maintaining indexes? Select all that apply.

options.text: Additional storage consumption
Extra work for relevant inserts, updates and deletes
Guaranteed faster writes
Potential maintenance overhead

questions.explanation: Indexes consume storage and need maintenance as table data changes. They can improve some reads, but they do not guarantee faster writes; write operations may become more expensive.

questions.prompt: A query returns most rows from a small table. Why might PostgreSQL choose a sequential scan even when a relevant index exists?

options.text: Indexes cannot be used on small tables
Fetching many rows through the index may cost more than scanning the table
A sequential scan always has a lower cost by definition
PostgreSQL ignores indexes after the first query

questions.explanation: An index is not automatically the cheapest route. When a large fraction of rows must be read, index navigation plus fetching many table rows can cost more than reading the table sequentially.

questions.prompt: Given a PostgreSQL B-tree index on (customer_id, created_at), which query pattern most directly matches the leading column?

options.text: Filtering by customer_id and ordering by created_at
Filtering only by an unrelated column called status
Filtering only by a completely different table's primary key
Any query, regardless of its predicates

questions.explanation: The index begins with customer_id, so queries that constrain that leading column and then use created_at can often benefit. Actual usefulness still depends on the full query, sort direction, predicates and planner estimates.

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the statement being analyzed.
questions.explanation: EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs the statement and reports actual execution information in addition to the plan. Be cautious with statements that modify data or with queries that are expensive to run.

questions.prompt: Which practices help you decide whether an index is useful? Select all that apply.

options.text: Inspect the actual query and its filtering or ordering pattern
Review the execution plan
Measure representative performance before and after a change
Add an index to every column without measuring

questions.explanation: Good index design starts from real query patterns, uses execution plans to understand current behavior, and validates improvements through measurement. Indexing every column blindly can increase storage and write costs.

questions.prompt: Where does a PostgreSQL index live?

options.text: As persistent database pages on storage; frequently used pages may also be cached in shared_buffers and the OS page cache
Only in RAM; a restart deletes it
Only inside the table's heap pages
Only in the SQL query plan

questions.explanation: Indexes have persistent on-disk storage and can consume memory through caching. Cache residency is a performance state, not the index's only storage location.

questions.prompt: An index exists on `is_active`, and 90% of rows are active. Why might PostgreSQL choose a sequential scan?

options.text: Fetching most heap rows through the index may cost more than reading table pages in order
PostgreSQL ignores every Boolean index
A sequential scan cannot use MVCC
Indexes are never used for equality predicates

questions.explanation: If most rows match, index navigation plus scattered heap fetches can cost more than sequentially reading the table.

questions.prompt: What is an important difference between `EXPLAIN` and `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`?

options.text: EXPLAIN shows a planned path; EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the statement and reports measured results
EXPLAIN ANALYZE never executes SQL
EXPLAIN reports exact runtime rows without executing
They always return identical timings

questions.explanation: EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the statement, so take extra care with data-changing queries and production workloads.

questions.prompt: A table receives 5,000 inserts per second. What should be checked before adding several more indexes?

options.text: Read benefit versus index-maintenance work, WAL, storage, and cache pressure under representative writes
Only how short the index name is
Whether the query contains SELECT
Whether the table uses a foreign key

questions.explanation: Each applicable insert/update must maintain relevant indexes. Benchmark the whole workload, not only the read query.

interviewScenarios.prompt: A production query is slow even though an index exists on the column used in its WHERE clause. How would you investigate?
strongAnswerPoints: Inspect the exact query, parameters, and execution plan.
Compare estimated and actual row counts where safe using EXPLAIN ANALYZE.
Check whether the predicate is selective and whether the index matches the filter, sort, and join patterns.
Look for expensive row fetches, stale statistics, locks, I/O pressure, or other bottlenecks.
Test a targeted change on representative data and measure read and write effects.
pitfalls: Assuming an index must be used because it exists.
Adding another index before examining the plan.
Running expensive EXPLAIN ANALYZE queries on production without considering impact.
interviewScenarios.referenceAnswer: I would first capture the exact query and representative parameters, then inspect EXPLAIN to see the chosen plan. If safe, I would use EXPLAIN ANALYZE to compare estimated and actual rows and identify where time is spent. I would verify selectivity, statistics, predicate shape, composite-index column order, sorting and joins. I would also check whether the delay is caused by locking, I/O or another bottleneck. Only then would I test a targeted index or query rewrite and measure the result against representative workload data.

interviewScenarios.prompt: A million-row users table has an email lookup that returns one row and an active-user report that returns 900,000 rows. Explain how you would check whether indexes help each query.
strongAnswerPoints: Compare EXPLAIN plans and actual rows/buffers on representative data.
Explain that a selective email lookup may benefit from an index while the broad report may prefer a sequential scan.
Measure latency and write overhead before keeping an index.
pitfalls: Claiming every index scan is faster
Using a single synthetic query as proof of workload-wide benefit
interviewScenarios.referenceAnswer: I would test each query separately with representative parameters. An indexed equality lookup returning one row may avoid most heap work, while returning 90% of the table may make sequential access cheaper. I would compare plans, buffers, latency, and write cost before deciding.
